175	\Delta_{t} & :=\Sigma_{*}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(\Sigma_{t}-\Sigma_{*}\right) \Sigma_{*}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
176	\end{aligned}
177	\]

179	The theorem below shows that $\varepsilon_{t}, \Delta_{t} \rightarrow 0$ in spectral norm. Specifically, it shows that this convergence occurs exponentially quickly at a rate controlled by the quality of initialization and amount of regularization.
180	
181	Theorem 3.1 (Exponential convergence). Suppose that $p=\mathcal{N}\left(\mu_{*}, \Sigma_{*}\right)$ in Algorithm 1, and let $\alpha>0$ denote the minimum eigenvalue of the matrix $\Sigma_{*}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \Sigma_{0} \Sigma_{*}^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. For any fixed level of regularization $\lambda>0$, define
182	\[
183	\beta:=\min \left(\alpha, \frac{1+\lambda}{1+\lambda+\left\|\varepsilon_{0}\right\|^{2}}\right), \quad \delta:=\frac{\lambda \beta}{1+\lambda}
184	\]
185	where $\beta \in(0,1]$ measures the quality of initialization and $\delta \in(0,1)$ denotes a rate of decay. Then with probability 1 in the limit of infinite batch size $(B \rightarrow \infty)$, and for all $t \geq 0$, the normalized errors in eqs. (14-15) satisfy
186	\[
187	\begin{aligned}
188	\left\|\varepsilon_{t}\right\| & \leq(1-\delta)^{t}\left\|\varepsilon_{0}\right\| \\
189	\left\|\Delta_{t}\right\| & \leq(1-\delta)^{t}\left\|\Delta_{0}\right\|+t(1-\delta)^{t-1}\left\|\varepsilon_{0}\right\|^{2}
190	\end{aligned}
191	\]
192	
193	Before sketching the proof we make three remarks. First, these error bounds behave sensibly: they suggest that the updates converge more slowly when the learning rate is small (with $\lambda \ll 1$ ), when the variational mean is poorly initialized (with $\left\|\varepsilon_{0}\right\|^{2} \gg 1$ ), and/or when the initial estimate of the covariance is nearly singular (with $\alpha \ll 1$ ). Second, the theorem holds under very general conditions-not only for any initialization of $\mu_{0}$ and $\Sigma_{0} \succ 0$, but also for any $\lambda>0$. This robustness is typical of proximal algorithms, which are well-known for their stability with respect to hyperparameters (Asi \& Duchi, 2019), but it is uncharacteristic of many gradient-based methods, which only converge when the learning rate varies inversely with the largest eigenvalue of an underlying Hessian (Garrigos \& Gower, 2023). Third, with more elaborate bookkeeping, we can derive tighter bounds both for the above setting and also when different iterations use varying levels of regularization $\left\{\lambda_{t}\right\}_{t=0}^{\infty}$. We give a full proof with these extensions in Appendix D.

196	\[
197	\begin{aligned}

199	\left\|\Delta_{t+1}\right\| & \leq(1-\delta)\left\|\Delta_{t}\right\|+\left\|\varepsilon_{t}\right\|^{2}
200	\end{aligned}
201	\]
202	where $\delta$ is given by eq. (16), and from these bounds, we use induction to prove the overall rates of decay in eqs. (17-18). Here we briefly describe the steps that are needed to derive the bounds in eqs. (19-20).

This limit is simplifying because by the law of large numbers, we can replace the batched averages over $B$ samples at each iteration by their expected values under the variational distribution $q_{t}=\mathcal{N}\left(\mu_{t}, \Sigma_{t}\right)$. 204	of the normalized mean $\varepsilon_{t}$ in eq. (14) and the normalized covariance matrix
205	\[
206	J_{t}=\Sigma_{*}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \Sigma_{t} \Sigma_{*}^{-\frac{1}{2}}=I+\Delta_{t}
207	\]
208	where $I$ denotes the identity matrix. In the infinite batch limit, we show that with probability 1 these quantities satisfy

210	\begin{array}{r}
211	\lambda J_{t+1}\left(J_{t}+\frac{1}{1+\lambda} \varepsilon_{t} \varepsilon_{t}^{\top}\right) J_{t+1}+J_{t+1}=(1+\lambda) J_{t} \\
212	\varepsilon_{t+1}=\left(I-\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda} J_{t+1}\right) \varepsilon_{t}
213	\end{array}

217	\[
218	\begin{aligned}
219	\lambda H_{t+1}\left(J_{t}+\frac{\left\|\varepsilon_{t}\right\|^{2}}{1+\lambda} I\right) H_{t+1}+H_{t+1} & =(1+\lambda) J_{t} \\
220	\lambda K_{t+1} J_{t} K_{t+1}+K_{t+1} & =(1+\lambda) J_{t}

226	H_{t+1} \preceq J_{t+1} \preceq K_{t+1}

230	\section*{4. Related work}
231	
232	BaM builds on intuitions from earlier work on Gaussian score matching (GSM) (Modi et al., 2023). GSM is an iterative algorithm for BBVI that updates a full-covariance Gaussian by analytically solving a system of nonlinear equations. As previously discussed, BaM recovers GSM as a special limiting case. A limitation of GSM is that it aims to match the scores exactly; thus, if the target is not exactly Gaussian, the updates for GSM attempt to solve an infeasible problem, In addition, the batch updates for GSM perform an ad hoc averaging that is not guaranteed to match any scores exactly, even when it is possible to do so. BaM overcomes these limitations by optimizing a proper score-based divergence on each batch of samples. Empirically, with BaM, we observe that larger batch sizes lead to more stable convergence. The score-based divergence behind BaM also lends itself to analysis, and we can provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence of BaM for Gaussian targets.
233	
234	Proximal point methods have been studied in several papers in the context of variational inference; typically the objective is a stochastic estimate of the ELBO with a (forward)
235	
236	KL regularization term. For example, Theis \& Hoffman (2015) optimize this objective using alternating coordinate ascent. In other work, Khan et al. $(2015 ; 2016)$ propose a splitting method for this objective, and by linearizing the difficult terms, they obtain a closed-form solution when the variational family is Gaussian and additional knowledge is given about the structure of the target. By contrast, BaM does not resort to linearization in order to obtain an analytical solution, nor does it require additional assumptions on the structure of the target.
237	
238	Proximal algorithms have also been developed for Gaussian variational families based on the Wasserstein metric. Lambert et al. (2022) consider a KL objective with the Wasserstein metric as a regularizer; in this case, the proximal step is not solvable in closed form. On the other hand, Diao et al. (2023) consider a proximal-gradient method, and show that the proximal step admits a closed-form solution.
239	Several works consider score matching with a Fisher divergence in the context of VI. For instance, Yu \& Zhang (2023) propose a score-matching approach for semi-implicit variational families based on stochastic gradient optimization of the Fisher divergence. Zhang et al. (2018) use the Fisher divergence with an energy-based model as the variational family. BaM differs from these approaches by working with a Gaussian variational family and an affine-invariant score-based divergence.
240	Finally, we note that the idea of score matching (Hyvärinen, 2005) with a (weighted) Fisher divergence appears in many contexts beyond VI (Song \& Ermon, 2019; Barp et al., 2019). One such context is generative modeling: here, given a set of training examples, the goal is to approximate an unknown data distribution $p$ by a parameterized model $p_{\theta}$ with an intractable normalization constant. Note that in this setting one can evaluate $\nabla \log p_{\theta}$ but not $\nabla \log p$. This setting is quite different from the setting of VI in this paper where we do not have samples from $p$, where we can evaluate $\nabla \log p$, and where the approximating distribution $q$ has the much simpler and more tractable form of a multivariate Gaussian.
241	
242	\section*{5. Experiments}
243	
244	We evaluate BaM against two other BBVI methods for Gaussian variational families with full covariance matrices. The first of these is automatic differentiation VI (ADVI) (Kucukelbir et al., 2017), which is based on ELBO maximization, and the second is GSM (Modi et al., 2023), as described in the previous section. We implement all algorithms using JAX (Bradbury et al., 2018), ${ }^{1}$ which supports efficient automatic differentiation both on CPU and GPU. We provide pseudocode for these methods in Appendix E.1.

253	\subsection*{5.1. Synthetically-constructed target distributions}
254	
255	We first validate BaM in two settings where we know the true target distribution $p$. In the first setting, we construct Gaussian targets with increasing number of dimensions. In the second setting, we study BaM for distributions with increasing (but controlled) amounts of non-Gaussianity. As evaluation metrics, we use empirical estimates of the KL divergence in both the forward direction, $\operatorname{KL}(p ; q)$, and the reverse direction, $\operatorname{KL}(q ; p)$.
256	
257	Gaussian targets with increasing dimensions. We construct Gaussian targets of increasing dimension with $D=$ $4,16,64,256$. In Figure 5.1, we compare BaM, ADVI, and GSM on each of these target distributions, plotting the forward KL divergence against the number of gradient evaluations; here we also consider two modified ADVI methods, where instead of the ELBO loss, we use the score-based divergence (labeled as "Score") and the Fisher divergence (labeled as "Fisher"). Results for the reverse KL divergence and other parameter settings are provided in Appendix E.3. In all of these experiments, we use a constant learning rate $\lambda_{t}=B D$ for BaM . Overall, we find that BaM converges orders of magnitude faster than ADVI. While GSM is competitive with BAM in some experiments, BaM converges more quickly with increasing batch size; this is unlike GSM which was observed to have marginal gains beyond $B=2$ for Gaussian targets (Modi et al., 2023).
258	We also observe that the gradient-based methods (ADVI, Score, Fisher) have similar performance in terms of convergence, and the score-based divergence is typically more sensitive to the learning rate. In Appendix E.2, we present wallclock timings for the methods, which show that the gradient evaluations dominate the computational cost in lower-dimensional settings.
259	
260	Non-Gaussian targets with varying skew and tails. The sinh-arcsinh normal distribution transforms a Gaussian random variable via the hyperbolic sine function and its inverse (Jones \& Pewsey, 2009; 2019). If $y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$, then a sample from the sinh-arcsinh normal distribution is
261	\[
262	z=\sinh \left(\frac{1}{\tau}\left(\sinh ^{-1}(y)+s\right)\right)
263	\]
264	where the parameters $s \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\tau>0$ control, respectively, the skew and the heaviness of the tails. The Gaussian distribution is recovered when $s=0$ and $\tau=1$.
265	We construct different non-Gaussian target distributions by varying these parameters. The results are presented in Figure 5.2 and Figure E.4. Here we use a decaying learning rate $\lambda_{t}=B D /(t+1)$ for BaM , as some decay is necessary for BaM to converge when the target distribution is nonGaussian.
266	
267	First, we construct target distributions with normal tails ( $t=1$ ) but varying skew ( $s=0.2,1.0,1.8$ ). Here we observe that BaM converges faster than ADVI. For large skew ( $s=1.0,1.8$ ), BaM converges to a higher value of the forward KL divergence but to similar values of the reverse KL divergence. In these experiments, we see that GSM and ADVI often have similar performance but that BaM stabilizes more quickly with larger batch sizes. Notably, the reverse KL divergence for GSM diverges when the target distribution is highly skewed ( $s=1.8$ ). The Score method diverges for highly skewed targets as well, and we found this method to be more sensitive to the learning rate.
268	
269	Next we construct target distributions with no skew ( $s=0$ ) but tails of varying heaviness $(t=0.1,0.9,1.7)$. Here we find that all methods tend to converge to similar values of the reverse KL divergence. In some cases, BaM and ADVI converge to better values than GSM, and BaM typically converges in fewer gradient evaluations than ADVI.

271	\subsection*{5.2. Application: hierarchical Bayesian models}
272	
273	We now consider the application of BaM to posterior inference. Suppose we have observations $\left\{x_{n}\right\}_{n=1}^{N}$, and the target distribution is the posterior density
274	\[
275	p\left(z \mid\left\{x_{n}\right\}_{n=1}^{N}\right) \propto p(z) p\left(\left\{x_{n}\right\}_{n=1}^{N} \mid z\right)
276	\]
277	with prior $p(z)$ and likelihood $p\left(\left\{x_{n}\right\}_{n=1}^{N} \mid z\right)$. We examine three target distributions from posteriordb (Magnusson et al., 2022), a database of Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017; Roualdes et al., 2023) models with reference samples generated using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC). The first target is nearly Gaussian (ark, D=7). The other

286	\subsection*{5.3. Application: deep generative model}
287	
288	In a deep generative model, the likelihood is parameterized by the output of a neural network $\Omega$, e.g.,
289	\[
290	\begin{aligned}
291	z_{n} & \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \\
292	x_{n} \mid z_{n} & \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\Omega\left(z_{n}, \hat{\theta}\right), \sigma^{2} I\right),
293	\end{aligned}
294	\]
295	where $x_{n}$ corresponds to a high-dimensional object, such as an image, and $z_{n}$ is a low-dimensional representation of $x_{n}$. The neural network $\Omega$ is parameterized by $\hat{\theta}$ and maps $z_{n}$ to the mean of the likelihood $p\left(x_{n} \mid z_{n}\right)$. For this example, we set $\sigma^{2}=0.1$. The above joint distribution underlies many deep learning models (Tomczak, 2022), including the variational autoencoder (Kingma \& Welling, 2014; Rezende et al., 2014). We train the neural network on the CIFAR-10 image data set (Krizhevsky, 2009). We model the images as continuous, with $x_{n} \in \mathbb{R}^{3072}$, and learn a latent representation $z_{n} \in \mathbb{R}^{256}$; see Appendix E. 6 for details.
296	
297	Given a new observation $x^{\prime}$, we wish to approximate the posterior $p\left(z^{\prime} \mid x^{\prime}\right)$. As an evaluation metric, we examine
298	how well $x^{\prime}$ is reconstructed by feeding the posterior expectation $\mathbb{E}\left[z^{\prime} \mid x^{\prime}\right]$ into the neural network $\Omega(\cdot, \hat{\theta})$. The quality of the reconstruction is assessed visually and using the mean squared error (MSE, Figure 5.4); we present the MSE plotted against wallclock time in Figure E.7. For ADVI and BaM , we use a pilot run of $T=100$ iterations to find a suitable learning rate; we then run the algorithms for $T=1000$ iterations. (GSM does not require this tuning step.) BaM performs poorly when the batch size is very small $(B=10)$ relative to the dimension of the latent variable $z^{\prime}$, but it becomes competitive as the batch size is increased. When the batch size is comparable to the dimension of $z_{n}$ (i.e. $B=300$ ), BaM converges an order of magnitude (or more) faster than ADVI and GSM.
299	
300	To refine our comparison, suppose we have a computational budget of 3000 gradient evaluations. Under this budget, ADVI achieves its lowest MSE for $B=10$ and $T=300$, while BaM produces a comparable result for $B=300$ and $T=10$. Hence, the gradient evaluations for BaM can be largely parallelized. By contrast, most gradients for ADVI must be evaluated sequentially. Notably, Figure E. 7 shows that BaM with $B=300$ converges faster in wallclock time.
301	Depending on how the parameter $\hat{\theta}$ of the neural network is estimated, it possible to learn an encoder and perform amortized variational inference (AVI) on a new observation $x^{\prime}$. When such an encoder is available, estimations of $p\left(z^{\prime} \mid x^{\prime}\right)$ can be obtained essentially for free. In our experiment, both BaM and ADVI eventually achieve a lower reconstruction error than AVI. This result is expected because our AVI implementation uses a factorized Gaussian approximation, whereas BaM and ADVI use a full-covariance approximation, and the latter provides better compression of $x^{\prime}$ even though the dimension of $z^{\prime}$ and the weights of the neural network remain unchanged.

303	\section*{6. Discussion and future work}
304	
305	In this paper, we introduce a score-based divergence that is especially well-suited to BBVI with Gaussian variational families. We show that the score-based divergence has a number of desirable properties. We then propose a regular-

We analyze the convergence of score-based BBVI when the target is Gaussian, and in the limit of an infinite batch size, we show that the updates converge exponentially quickly to the target mean and covariance. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of BaM in a number of empirical studies involving both Gaussian and non-Gaussian targets; here we observe that for sufficiently large batch sizes, our method converges much faster than other BBVI algorithms.

314	There are a number of fruitful directions for future work. First, it remains to analyze the convergence of BaM in the finite-batch case and for a larger class of target distributions. Second, it seems promising to develop score-based BBVI
315	for other (non-Gaussian) variational families, and more generally, to study what divergences lend themselves to stochastic proximal point algorithms. Third, the BaM approach can be modified to utilize data subsampling (potentially with control variates (Wang et al., 2024)) for large-scale Bayesian inference problems, where a noisy estimate of the target density's score is used in place of its exact score.

\section*{E.2. Wallclock timings}

In the main paper, we report the number of gradient evaluations as a measure of the cost of the algorithm. While the complete cost is not captured by the number of gradient evaluations alone, here we show that the computational cost of the algorithms are dominated by gradient evaluations, and so number of gradient evaluations is a good proxy of the computational cost. We additionally note that all work with full covariance matrices make a basic assumption that $\mathcal{O}\left(D^{2}\right)$ is not prohibitive because there are $\mathcal{O}\left(D^{2}\right)$ parameters in the model itself. While the BaM update (when $B \geq D$ ) takes $\mathcal{O}\left(D^{3}\right)$ computation per iteration, in this setting, $\mathcal{O}\left(D^{3}\right)$ is not generally regarded as prohibitive in models where there are $\mathcal{O}\left(D^{2}\right)$ parameters to estimate.

In Figure E.1, we plot the wallclock timings for Gaussian targets of increasing dimension, where $D=4,16,64,128,256$. We observe that for dimensions 64 and under, all methods have similar timings; for the larger dimensions, we observe that the low-rank BaM solver has a similar timing. All experiments in the paper fit into the lower-dimensional regime or the low-rank regime, with the exception of the deep generative models application, which includes larger batch sizes. Thus, for the lower-dimensional regime and the low-rank examples, we report the number of gradient evaluations as the primary measure of cost; the cost per iteration for the mini-batch regime is $\mathcal{O}\left(D^{2} B+B^{3}\right)$. For the deep generative model example, we additionally report in Figure E. 7 the wallclock timings. We note that the wallclock timings themselves are heavily dependent on implementation and JIT-compilation details and hardware.

\section*{E.3. Gaussian target}

Each target distribution was generated randomly; here the covariance was constructed by generating a $D \times D$ matrix $A$ and computing $\Sigma_{*}=A A^{\top}$.

For all experiments, the algorithms were initialized with $\mu_{0} \sim$ uniform $[0,0.1]$ and $\Sigma_{0}=I$. In Figure E.3, we report the results for the reverse KL divergence. We observe largely the same conclusions as with the forward KL divergence presented in Section 5.

In addition, we evaluated BaM with a number of different schedules for the learning rates: $\lambda_{t}=B, B D, \frac{B}{t+1}, \frac{B D}{t+1}$. We show one such example for $D=16$ in Figure E.2, where each figure represents a particular choice of $\lambda_{t}$, and where each line is the mean over 10 runs. For the constant learning rate, the lines for $B=20,40$ are on top of each other. Here we observe that the constant learning rates perform the best for Gaussian targets. For the gradient-based methods (ADVI, Score, Fisher), the learning rate was set by choosing the best value over a grid search. For ADVI and Fisher, the selected learning rate was 0.01. Here we again consider the sinh-arcsinh distribution with $D=10$, where we vary the skew and tails. We present the reverse KL results in Figure E.4.

All algorithms were initialized with a random initial mean $\mu_{0}$ and $\Sigma_{0}=I$. Unlike for Gaussian targets, we found that constant $\lambda_{t}$ did not perform as well as those with a varying schedule. In Bayesian posterior inference applications, it is common to measure the relative mean error and the relative standard deviation error (Welandawe et al., 2022):
\[
\text { relative mean error }=\left\|\frac{\mu-\hat{\mu}}{\sigma}\right\|_{2}, \quad \text { relative } \mathrm{SD} \text { error }=\left\|\frac{\sigma-\hat{\sigma}}{\sigma}\right\|_{2}
\]
where $\hat{\mu}, \hat{\sigma}$ are computed from the variational distribution, and $\mu, \sigma$ are the posterior mean and standard deviation. We estimated the posterior mean and standard deviation using the reference samples from HMC.

In the evaluation, all algorithms were initialized with $\mu_{0} \sim$ uniform $[0,0.1]$ and $\Sigma_{0}=I$. The results for the relative mean error are presented in Section 5. In Figure E.6, we present the results for the relative SD error. """Core implementations: BaM, GSM, ADVI (ELBO / score-divergence / Fisher-divergence losses).

All algorithms are written as a pure `step(state, key, t)` function so that many
iterations can be jitted/vmapped. Each iteration of every method consumes B score
(gradient) evaluations of the target, which is the x-axis used throughout.
"""
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import optax
from functools import partial

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- BaM
def bam_update(mu, Sigma, z, g, lam):
    """One BaM match step (Algorithm 1, eqs. 10-13) given samples z (B,D) and scores g (B,D)."""
    B, D = z.shape
    zbar = z.mean(0)
    gbar = g.mean(0)
    zc = z - zbar
    gc = g - gbar
    C = zc.T @ zc / B
    Gam = gc.T @ gc / B
    U = lam * Gam + lam / (1 + lam) * jnp.outer(gbar, gbar)
    dm = mu - zbar
    V = Sigma + lam * C + lam / (1 + lam) * jnp.outer(dm, dm)
    V = 0.5 * (V + V.T)
    # Sigma_new = 2 V (I + (I + 4UV)^{1/2})^{-1}
    #           = V^{1/2} Q diag(2 / (1 + sqrt(1 + 4 w))) Q^T V^{1/2},  W = V^{1/2} U V^{1/2} = Q diag(w) Q^T
    ev, EV = jnp.linalg.eigh(V)
    ev = jnp.clip(ev, 1e-300, None)
    Vh = (EV * jnp.sqrt(ev)) @ EV.T
    W = Vh @ U @ Vh
    W = 0.5 * (W + W.T)
    w, Q = jnp.linalg.eigh(W)
    w = jnp.clip(w, 0.0, None)
    M = (Q * (2.0 / (1.0 + jnp.sqrt(1.0 + 4.0 * w)))) @ Q.T
    Snew = Vh @ M @ Vh
    Snew = 0.5 * (Snew + Snew.T)
    munew = mu / (1 + lam) + lam / (1 + lam) * (Snew @ gbar + zbar)
    return munew, Snew


def sample_gauss(key, mu, Sigma, B):
    L = jnp.linalg.cholesky(Sigma)
    eps = jax.random.normal(key, (B, mu.shape[0]))
    return mu + eps @ L.T


def make_bam(score_fn, B, lr_schedule):
    """lr_schedule(t) -> lambda_t (e.g. B*D constant or B*D/(t+1))."""
    vscore = jax.vmap(score_fn)

    def init(mu0, Sigma0):
        return dict(mu=mu0, Sigma=Sigma0)

    def step(state, key, t):
        z = sample_gauss(key, state["mu"], state["Sigma"], B)
        g = vscore(z)
        mu, S = bam_update(state["mu"], state["Sigma"], z, g, lr_schedule(t))
        # guard against numerical failure: keep previous state if nan
        ok = jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(mu)) & jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(S))
        mu = jnp.where(ok, mu, state["mu"])
        S = jnp.where(ok, S, state["Sigma"])
        return dict(mu=mu, Sigma=S)

    get = lambda s: (s["mu"], s["Sigma"])
    return init, step, get


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- GSM
def gsm_update(mu, Sigma, z, s):
    """GSM (Modi et al. 2023) batch update, Algorithm 3 of the paper."""

    def one(zb, sb):
        eps = Sigma @ sb - mu + zb
        dz = mu - zb
        a = sb @ Sigma @ sb + (dz @ sb) ** 2
        rho = 0.5 * (-1.0 + jnp.sqrt(1.0 + 4.0 * a))
        denom = 1.0 + rho + dz @ sb
        dmu = (eps - dz * (sb @ eps) / denom) / (1.0 + rho)
        mut = mu + dmu
        dS = jnp.outer(dz, dz) - jnp.outer(mut - zb, mut - zb)
        return dmu, dS

    dmu, dS = jax.vmap(one)(z, s)
    return mu + dmu.mean(0), Sigma + dS.mean(0)


def make_gsm(score_fn, B):
    vscore = jax.vmap(score_fn)

    def init(mu0, Sigma0):
        return dict(mu=mu0, Sigma=Sigma0)

    def step(state, key, t):
        z = sample_gauss(key, state["mu"], state["Sigma"], B)
        g = vscore(z)
        mu, S = gsm_update(state["mu"], state["Sigma"], z, g)
        S = 0.5 * (S + S.T)
        # reject updates that break positive definiteness / produce nans
        ok = jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(mu)) & jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(S)) & jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(jnp.linalg.cholesky(S)))
        mu = jnp.where(ok, mu, state["mu"])
        S = jnp.where(ok, S, state["Sigma"])
        return dict(mu=mu, Sigma=S)

    get = lambda s: (s["mu"], s["Sigma"])
    return init, step, get


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- ADVI family
def _L_from(params):
    Lraw = params["L"]
    D = Lraw.shape[0]
    Lt = jnp.tril(Lraw, -1)
    d = jax.nn.softplus(jnp.diag(Lraw))
    return Lt + jnp.diag(d)


def _inv_softplus(x):
    return jnp.log(jnp.expm1(x))


def make_advi(logp_fn, score_fn, B, lr, loss="elbo"):
    """Reparameterised gradient-based BBVI with ADAM. loss in {elbo, score, fisher}.

    Sigma = L L^T with L lower-triangular (softplus diagonal).
    - elbo:   -1/B sum_b [log p(z_b) - log q(z_b)]                       (Algorithm 2)
    - score:  1/B sum_b || grad log q(z_b) - grad log p(z_b) ||^2_{Sigma}  (score-based divergence)
    - fisher: 1/B sum_b || grad log q(z_b) - grad log p(z_b) ||^2_{I}      (Fisher divergence)
    """
    opt = optax.adam(lr)
    vlogp = jax.vmap(logp_fn)
    vscore = jax.vmap(score_fn)

    def loss_fn(params, eps):
        mu = params["mu"]
        L = _L_from(params)
        z = mu + eps @ L.T
        if loss == "elbo":
            logdet = jnp.sum(jnp.log(jnp.diag(L)))
            logq = -0.5 * jnp.sum(eps ** 2, 1) - logdet
            return -jnp.mean(vlogp(z) - logq)
        sp = vscore(z)
        # grad log q(z) = -Sigma^{-1}(z-mu) = -L^{-T} eps
        sq = -jax.scipy.linalg.solve_triangular(L.T, eps.T, lower=False).T
        diff = sq - sp
        if loss == "score":
            Ld = diff @ L  # ||d||^2_Sigma = ||L^T d||^2
            return jnp.mean(jnp.sum(Ld ** 2, 1))
        return jnp.mean(jnp.sum(diff ** 2, 1))

    def init(mu0, Sigma0):
        L0 = jnp.linalg.cholesky(Sigma0)
        Lraw = jnp.tril(L0, -1) + jnp.diag(_inv_softplus(jnp.diag(L0)))
        params = dict(mu=mu0, L=Lraw)
        return dict(params=params, opt=opt.init(params))

    def step(state, key, t):
        D = state["params"]["mu"].shape[0]
        eps = jax.random.normal(key, (B, D))
        l, gr = jax.value_and_grad(loss_fn)(state["params"], eps)
        upd, os = opt.update(gr, state["opt"], state["params"])
        newp = optax.apply_updates(state["params"], upd)
        ok = jnp.isfinite(l) & jax.tree_util.tree_reduce(lambda a, b: a & b, jax.tree_util.tree_map(lambda x: jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(x)), newp))
        newp = jax.tree_util.tree_map(lambda a, b: jnp.where(ok, a, b), newp, state["params"])
        return dict(params=newp, opt=os)

    def get(s):
        L = _L_from(s["params"])
        return s["params"]["mu"], L @ L.T

    return init, step, get


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- runner
def run_method(method, init, step, get, mu0s, Sigma0, key, n_iters, B, ckpt_iters, metric_fn):
    """Run `n_seeds` independent chains (vmapped) and evaluate metric_fn(mu, Sigma, key) at checkpoints.

    ckpt_iters: sorted array of iteration counts at which to evaluate (0 allowed).
    Returns grad_evals (n_ckpt,), metrics (n_seeds, n_ckpt) [metric_fn may return tuple -> dict]
    """
    n_seeds = mu0s.shape[0]
    states = jax.vmap(lambda m: init(m, Sigma0))(mu0s)
    keys = jax.random.split(key, n_seeds)

    @jax.jit
    def advance(states, keys, t0, n):
        def body(i, carry):
            st, ks = carry
            t = t0 + i
            sub = jax.vmap(lambda k: jax.random.fold_in(k, t))(ks)
            st = jax.vmap(lambda s, k: step(s, k, t))(st, sub)
            return st, ks

        st, _ = jax.lax.fori_loop(0, n, body, (states, keys))
        return st

    vmetric = jax.jit(jax.vmap(lambda s, k: metric_fn(*get(s), k)))
    out = []
    t = 0
    mkey = jax.random.PRNGKey(12345)
    for c in ckpt_iters:
        n = int(c) - t
        if n > 0:

import argparse, json, os, time

import jax, jax.numpy as jnp

p.add_argument("--seeds", type=int, default=5)
p.add_argument("--grid_seeds", type=int, default=2)
p.add_argument("--budget", type=int, default=100000)

p.add_argument("--out", default="results/posteriordb")

def load_draws(name):
    d = json.load(open(os.path.join(PDB, name)))
    keys = list(d[0].keys())
    return {k: np.concatenate([np.asarray(c[k]) for c in d]) for k in keys}


def model_ark():
    dat = json.load(open(os.path.join(PDB, "arK.json")))
    K, T, y = dat["K"], dat["T"], jnp.asarray(dat["y"])
    X = jnp.stack([y[K - k - 1:T - k - 1] for k in range(K)], 1)  # y[t-k], t=K..T-1 (k=1..K)
    yt = y[K:]

    def logp(th):
        alpha, beta, lsig = th[0], th[1:1 + K], th[1 + K]
        sig = jnp.exp(lsig)
        lp = norm.logpdf(alpha, 0, 10) + jnp.sum(norm.logpdf(beta, 0, 10)) + cauchy.logpdf(sig, 0, 2.5) + lsig
        return lp + jnp.sum(norm.logpdf(yt, alpha + X @ beta, sig))

    dr = load_draws("arK-arK.json")

    ref = np.concatenate([np.log(dr["rho"])[:, None], np.log(dr["alpha"])[:, None], ft], 1)
    return logp, ref

        return lp + jnp.sum(norm.logpdf(y, theta, sig))

"""Section 5.3: deep generative model (VAE decoder trained on CIFAR-10), posterior inference over z' in R^256.

Reduced-compute version: the VAE is trained for a few epochs on CPU (paper: 100 epochs), and the
BBVI methods are run for fewer iterations (paper: T=1000).
"""
import argparse, json, os, pickle, time
import numpy as np
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp
import optax
import flax.linen as nn
from bam_lib import make_bam, make_gsm, make_advi, run_method

p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--epochs", type=int, default=3)
p.add_argument("--ntrain", type=int, default=50000)
p.add_argument("--c_hid", type=int, default=32)
p.add_argument("--T", type=int, default=300)
p.add_argument("--n_images", type=int, default=1)
p.add_argument("--seeds", type=int, default=2)
p.add_argument("--out", default="results/vae")
a = p.parse_args()
os.makedirs(a.out, exist_ok=True)
HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
LATENT, SIG2 = 256, 0.1


def load_cifar():
    d = os.path.join(HERE, "data", "cifar", "cifar-10-batches-py")
    xs = []
    for i in range(1, 6):
        xs.append(pickle.load(open(os.path.join(d, f"data_batch_{i}"), "rb"), encoding="bytes")[b"data"])
    tr = np.concatenate(xs)
    te = pickle.load(open(os.path.join(d, "test_batch"), "rb"), encoding="bytes")[b"data"]
    f = lambda x: (x.reshape(-1, 3, 32, 32).transpose(0, 2, 3, 1).astype(np.float32) / 255.0) * 2 - 1
    return f(tr), f(te)


class Encoder(nn.Module):
    c: int

    @nn.compact
    def __call__(self, x):
        c = self.c
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(c, (3, 3), strides=2)(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(c, (3, 3), strides=1)(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(2 * c, (3, 3), strides=2)(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(2 * c, (3, 3), strides=1)(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(2 * c, (3, 3), strides=2)(x))
        x = x.reshape(x.shape[0], -1)
        return nn.Dense(LATENT)(x), nn.Dense(LATENT)(x)  # mean, log-variance (factorized Gaussian)


class Decoder(nn.Module):
    c: int

    @nn.compact
    def __call__(self, z):
        c = self.c
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Dense(4 * 4 * 2 * c)(z)).reshape(z.shape[0], 4, 4, 2 * c)
        x = nn.gelu(nn.ConvTranspose(2 * c, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2))(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(2 * c, (3, 3))(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.ConvTranspose(c, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2))(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(c, (3, 3))(x))
        return jnp.tanh(nn.ConvTranspose(3, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2))(x))


xtr, xte = load_cifar()
xtr = xtr[: a.ntrain]
enc, dec = Encoder(a.c_hid), Decoder(a.c_hid)
ckpt = os.path.join(a.out, "vae_params.pkl")
if os.path.exists(ckpt):
    params = pickle.load(open(ckpt, "rb"))
else:
    k = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
    params = {"enc": enc.init(k, xtr[:1]), "dec": dec.init(k, jnp.zeros((1, LATENT)))}
    bs = 128
    steps = a.epochs * (len(xtr) // bs)
    sched = optax.warmup_cosine_decay_schedule(0.0, 1e-3, 100, steps, 1e-5)
    opt = optax.adam(sched)
    ost = opt.init(params)

    def neg_elbo(params, x, key):  # 1 MC sample
        m, lv = enc.apply(params["enc"], x)
        z = m + jnp.exp(0.5 * lv) * jax.random.normal(key, m.shape)
        xh = dec.apply(params["dec"], z)
        ll = -0.5 * jnp.sum((x - xh) ** 2, (1, 2, 3)) / SIG2
        kl = 0.5 * jnp.sum(jnp.exp(lv) + m ** 2 - 1 - lv, 1)
        return jnp.mean(kl - ll)

    @jax.jit
    def train_step(params, ost, x, key):
        l, g = jax.value_and_grad(neg_elbo)(params, x, key)
        u, ost = opt.update(g, ost, params)
        return optax.apply_updates(params, u), ost, l

    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    it, t0, hist = 0, time.time(), []
    for ep in range(a.epochs):
        perm = rng.permutation(len(xtr))
        for i in range(len(xtr) // bs):
            params, ost, l = train_step(params, ost, xtr[perm[i * bs:(i + 1) * bs]], jax.random.PRNGKey(it))
            it += 1
            if it % 100 == 0:
                hist.append((it, float(l)))
                print(f"epoch {ep} step {it}/{steps} negELBO {float(l):.1f} ({time.time()-t0:.0f}s)", flush=True)
    pickle.dump(params, open(ckpt, "wb"))
    json.dump(hist, open(os.path.join(a.out, "train_hist.json"), "w"))

pd = jax.tree_util.tree_map(lambda x: jnp.asarray(x, jnp.float64), params["dec"])
results = {}
for img in range(a.n_images):
    x = jnp.asarray(xte[img], jnp.float64)

    def logp(z):
        xh = dec.apply(pd, z[None])[0]
        return -0.5 * jnp.sum((x - xh) ** 2) / SIG2 - 0.5 * jnp.sum(z ** 2)

    score = jax.grad(logp)
    recon = jax.jit(lambda z: dec.apply(pd, z[None])[0])
    mse_fn = lambda mu, S, k: jnp.mean((recon(mu) - x) ** 2)
    m_avi, _ = enc.apply(params["enc"], xte[img:img + 1])
    avi_mse = float(jnp.mean((recon(jnp.asarray(m_avi[0], jnp.float64)) - x) ** 2))
    print(f"image {img}: AVI (encoder mean) MSE = {avi_mse:.4f}", flush=True)
    res = {"AVI_mse": avi_mse}
    mu0 = jnp.zeros((a.seeds, LATENT))
    S0 = jnp.eye(LATENT)

    def go(name, B, mk, T):
        init, step, get = mk(B)
        ck = np.unique(np.round(np.logspace(0, np.log10(T), 15)).astype(int))
        ck = np.concatenate([[0], ck])
        t0 = time.time()
        ge, m = run_method(name, init, step, get, mu0, S0, jax.random.PRNGKey(img), T, B, ck, mse_fn)
        print(f"image {img} {name}: final MSE {np.mean(m[:, -1]):.4f} min {np.min(np.mean(m,0)):.4f} ({time.time()-t0:.0f}s)", flush=True)
        return dict(grad_evals=ge.tolist(), mse=np.asarray(m).tolist(), B=B, T=T)

    # pilot runs (T=30) to choose learning rates, as in the paper (pilot T=100)
    def pilot(mk_lr, grid, B):
        best, bv = None, np.inf
        for lr in grid:
            r = go(f"pilot B={B} lr={lr}", B, lambda B: mk_lr(B, lr), 30)
            v = np.nanmean(np.asarray(r["mse"])[:, -1])
            if np.isfinite(v) and v < bv:
                best, bv = lr, v
        return best if best is not None else grid[0]

    for B in [10, 50, 300]:
        lam0 = pilot(lambda B, l: make_bam(score, B, lambda t, l=l: l), [1.0, 10.0, 100.0], B)
        res[f"BaM-{B}"] = go(f"BaM-{B} (lambda={lam0})", B, lambda B: make_bam(score, B, lambda t: lam0), a.T)
        res[f"BaM-{B}"]["lr"] = lam0
    for B in [10, 50]:
        lr = pilot(lambda B, l: make_advi(logp, score, B, l, "elbo"), [1e-3, 1e-2, 5e-2], B)
        res[f"ADVI-{B}"] = go(f"ADVI-{B} (lr={lr})", B, lambda B: make_advi(logp, score, B, lr, "elbo"), a.T)
        res[f"ADVI-{B}"]["lr"] = lr
    for B in [10, 50]:
        res[f"GSM-{B}"] = go(f"GSM-{B}", B, lambda B: make_gsm(score, B), a.T)
    results[img] = res
    np.save(os.path.join(a.out, f"x{img}.npy"), np.asarray(x))
    best_mu = {}
json.dump(results, open(os.path.join(a.out, "vae_results.json"), "w"))

"""Make figures + summary tables from results/*. Missing results are skipped."""
import json, os, glob
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

R = "results"
os.makedirs("figures", exist_ok=True)
COL = {"BaM": "#2a0a3a", "GSM": "#c2185b", "ADVI": "#f4a261", "Score": "#e63946", "Fisher": "#e76f51"}
summary = []


def col(name):
    for k, c in COL.items():
        if name.startswith(k):
            return c
    return "gray"


def style(name):
    if name.startswith("BaM"):
        return "-" if name.endswith(("5", "15", "40", "150", "10", "32", "300")) else "--"
    return "-"


def curve(ax, x, Y, name, ls=None, band=False):
    Y = np.asarray(Y, float)
    Yc = np.clip(Y, 1e-8, None)
    m = np.nanmean(Yc, 0)
    ax.plot(np.maximum(x, 1), m, ls or style(name), color=col(name), label=name, lw=1.8)
    if band and Y.shape[0] > 1:
        se = np.nanstd(Yc, 0) / np.sqrt(Y.shape[0])
        ax.fill_between(np.maximum(x, 1), np.clip(m - se, 1e-8, None), m + se, color=col(name), alpha=0.2)
    else:
        for y in Yc:
            ax.plot(np.maximum(x, 1), y, color=col(name), alpha=0.12, lw=0.6)


# --- Gaussian targets
files = sorted(glob.glob(f"{R}/gaussian/D*.json"), key=lambda f: int(f.split("D")[-1][:-5]))
for key, lab in [("fkl", "Forward KL"), ("rkl", "Reverse KL")]:
    if not files:
        break
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, len(files), figsize=(4 * len(files), 3.2))
    axs = np.atleast_1d(axs)
    for ax, f in zip(axs, files):
        D = f.split("D")[-1][:-5]
        res = json.load(open(f))
        for name, r in res.items():
            if name.startswith("_"):
                continue
            curve(ax, np.asarray(r["grad_evals"]), r[key], name)
            if key == "fkl":
                fin = np.asarray(r["fkl"], float)[:, -1]
                fr = np.asarray(r["rkl"], float)[:, -1]
                summary.append(f"| Gaussian D={D} | {name} | B={r['B']} | lr={r.get('lr', '-')} | {r['grad_evals'][-1]} | {np.nanmedian(fin):.3g} | {np.nanmedian(fr):.3g} |")
        ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_title(f"D={D}"); ax.set_xlabel("# gradient evaluations")
        ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    axs[0].set_ylabel(lab); axs[0].legend(fontsize=7)
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(f"figures/gaussian_{key}.png", dpi=120); plt.close()

# --- sinh-arcsinh
files = sorted(glob.glob(f"{R}/sinharcsinh/*.json"))
order = ["s0.2_t1.0", "s1.0_t1.0", "s1.8_t1.0", "s0.0_t0.1", "s0.0_t0.9", "s0.0_t1.7"]
files = [f"{R}/sinharcsinh/{o}.json" for o in order if os.path.exists(f"{R}/sinharcsinh/{o}.json")]
for key, lab in [("fkl", "Forward KL"), ("rkl", "Reverse KL")]:
    if not files:
        break
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, len(files), figsize=(3.3 * len(files), 3.2))
    axs = np.atleast_1d(axs)
    for ax, f in zip(axs, files):
        tag = os.path.basename(f)[:-5]
        res = json.load(open(f))
        for name, r in res.items():
            if name.startswith("_"):
                continue
            curve(ax, np.asarray(r["grad_evals"]), r[key], name, band=True)
            if key == "fkl":
                fin = np.asarray(r["fkl"], float)[:, -3:].mean(1)
                fr = np.asarray(r["rkl"], float)[:, -3:].mean(1)
                summary.append(f"| sinh-arcsinh {tag} | {name} | B={r['B']} | lr={r.get('lr', '-')} | {r['grad_evals'][-1]} | {np.nanmedian(fin):.3g} | {np.nanmedian(fr):.3g} |")
        ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_title(tag.replace("_t", ", tau=").replace("s", "s=", 1)); ax.set_xlabel("# gradient evaluations")
        ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    axs[0].set_ylabel(lab); axs[0].legend(fontsize=7)
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(f"figures/sinharcsinh_{key}.png", dpi=120); plt.close()

# --- posteriordb
names = [("ark", "Nearly Gaussian (arK)"), ("gp_pois_regr", "Gaussian process"), ("eight_schools_centered", "Hierarchical (8 schools)")]
names = [n for n in names if os.path.exists(f"{R}/posteriordb/{n[0]}.json")]
for key, lab in [("rel_mean", "Rel. mean error"), ("rel_sd", "Rel. SD error")]:
    if not names:
        break
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, len(names), figsize=(4.5 * len(names), 3.2))
    axs = np.atleast_1d(axs)
    for ax, (n, title) in zip(axs, names):
        res = json.load(open(f"{R}/posteriordb/{n}.json"))
        for name, r in res.items():
            ls = "-" if name.endswith("-32") else "--"
            curve(ax, np.asarray(r["grad_evals"]), r[key], name, ls=ls, band=True)
            if key == "rel_mean":
                summary.append(f"| posteriordb {n} | {name} | B={r['B']} | lr={r.get('lr', '-')} | {r['grad_evals'][-1]} | rel-mean {np.nanmean(np.asarray(r['rel_mean'])[:, -1]):.3g} | rel-SD {np.nanmean(np.asarray(r['rel_sd'])[:, -1]):.3g} |")
        ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("# gradient evaluations"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    axs[0].set_ylabel(lab); axs[0].legend(fontsize=7)
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(f"figures/posteriordb_{key}.png", dpi=120); plt.close()

# --- VAE
f = f"{R}/vae/vae_results.json"
if os.path.exists(f):
    allres = json.load(open(f))
    for img, res in allres.items():
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.5))
        for name, r in res.items():
            if name == "AVI_mse":
                ax.axhline(r, color="k", ls=":", label="AVI (encoder)")
                summary.append(f"| VAE img {img} | AVI | - | - | 0 | MSE {r:.4f} | |")
                continue
            m = np.asarray(r["mse"]).mean(0)
            ax.plot(np.maximum(r["grad_evals"], 1), m, "-" if name.startswith("BaM") else "--", color=col(name), label=name,
                    alpha=0.5 + 0.5 * (r["B"] / 300))
            ge = np.asarray(r["grad_evals"])
            within = ge <= 3000
            summary.append(f"| VAE img {img} | {name} | B={r['B']} | lr={r.get('lr', '-')} | {ge[-1]} | MSE final {m[-1]:.4f} | MSE@<=3000 evals {m[within].min():.4f} |")
        ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("# gradient evaluations"); ax.set_ylabel("reconstruction MSE"); ax.legend(fontsize=7); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
        plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(f"figures/vae_mse_img{img}.png", dpi=120); plt.close()

open("results/summary_table.md", "w").write(
    "| experiment | method | batch | lr | final #grad evals | metric 1 (fwd KL / rel-mean / MSE) | metric 2 (rev KL / rel-SD) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n" + "\n".join(summary) + "\n")
print("\n".join(summary))

# Reproduction: Batch and Match (BaM) — black-box VI with a score-based divergence

CPU-only JAX reimplementation of BaM (Algorithm 1), with the baselines from the paper: GSM (Algorithm 3),
ADVI (Algorithm 2, reparameterised ELBO + ADAM), and the "Score" / "Fisher" variants of ADVI (score-based /
Fisher divergence as the loss). I wrote all of the code from the paper's descriptions; the authors'
GSM-VI repository was not used.

## Files
- `bam_lib.py` contains the algorithms.
  - BaM update: eqs. (10)–(13). The covariance update `Σ = 2V(I+(I+4UV)^{1/2})^{-1}` is computed in the
    equivalent symmetric form `V^{1/2} Q diag(2/(1+sqrt(1+4w))) Q^T V^{1/2}`, where `Q diag(w) Q^T = V^{1/2} U V^{1/2}`.
  - GSM batch update.
  - ADVI / Score / Fisher with a Cholesky parameterisation (the diagonal goes through a softplus).
  - A vmapped/jitted runner that records metrics against the number of gradient evaluations (B per iteration).
- `exp_gaussian.py` covers Sec. 5.1, Gaussian targets: Σ* = AAᵀ, μ0 ~ U[0,0.1], Σ0 = I, BaM λ=BD. There is an
  ADAM learning-rate grid search for ADVI/Score/Fisher. It reports forward KL (Fig 5.1) and reverse KL (Fig E.3).
- `exp_sinharcsinh.py` covers Sec. 5.1, sinh-arcsinh targets with D=10, for (s,τ) ∈ {(0.2,1),(1,1),(1.8,1),(0,0.1),(0,0.9),(0,1.7)}.
  BaM uses λ_t = BD/(t+1). The gradient-based methods get a learning-rate grid search. It reports Monte-Carlo forward and reverse KL (Fig 5.2 / E.4).
- `exp_posteriordb.py` covers Sec. 5.2: arK (D=7), gp_pois_regr (D=13) and eight_schools_centered (D=10).
  - I re-implemented the Stan models in JAX on the unconstrained space, including the log-Jacobians, instead of using bridgestan.
  - The reference mean and SD come from the posteriordb HMC reference draws, mapped to the same unconstrained space and stored in `data/pdb/`.
  - For eight-schools, posteriordb only has reference draws for the non-centered version. Its (θ, μ, τ) have the same posterior.
  - It reports relative mean error (Fig 5.3) and relative SD error (Fig E.6) for B=8 and B=32. BaM uses λ_t = BD/(t+1), and ADVI gets an LR grid search.
- `exp_vae.py` covers Sec. 5.3: a CIFAR-10 VAE with the addendum architecture, then BaM/ADVI/GSM posterior inference
  in a 256-dimensional latent space, with AVI as a baseline. **It was written but not run in this session** (see below).
- `plot_all.py` writes `figures/*.png` and `results/summary_table.md`.
- `reproduce.sh` runs everything with the reduced settings used here.

## What was achieved / deviations
- **Gaussian targets:** D=4 and 16 ran in full (10 seeds, 4·10⁴ gradient evaluations). D=64 was started with
  reduced settings but did not finish before the time limit. D=256 was not run: the CPU was shared by 4 jobs and it
  was too slow. Its command is in `reproduce.sh` behind `RUN_D256=1`.
- **Sinh-arcsinh:** the (0.2, 1) target ran with 5 seeds and 10⁴ evaluations. The other targets were launched with
  5·10³ evaluations and a smaller LR grid. Whatever finished is in `results/sinharcsinh/`, and RESULTS.md says which.
  - The target is y ~ N(μ, AAᵀ+I). I added the +I so the covariance is well conditioned; with plain AAᵀ the
    s=0.2 target was already extremely non-Gaussian. The paper does not give its exact choice.
- **posteriordb:** ran with 5 seeds and a budget of 10⁵ gradient evaluations (the paper used ≈4·10⁵).
- **VAE (Sec 5.3):** the code was written, but it was not executed or verified. A smoke test on fake data did not
  finish within the time available. It is disabled by default in `reproduce.sh`; set `RUN_VAE=1` to try it.
- Wall-clock experiments are out of scope and were not done.

`reproduce.sh` regenerates `results/*.json`, `logs/*.log`, `figures/*.png` and `results/summary_table.md`.

# Results from this session

The complete per-method numbers are in `results/summary_table.md` and the figures are in `figures/`. All numbers
below come from runs in this session, on a CPU that was shared between several jobs. Because of the time limit,
the settings are reduced relative to the paper; README.md lists the deviations.

## Sec 5.1 — Gaussian targets (Fig 5.1 / E.3): D=4 and D=16, 10 seeds, 4·10⁴ gradient evaluations
`figures/gaussian_fkl.png`, `figures/gaussian_rkl.png`

| D | BaM-2 | BaM-big (B=5/15) | GSM (B=2) | ADVI | Score | Fisher |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4: evals to reach fwd KL < 1e-6 | ≈60 | ≈30 | ≈100 | never (final 2e-3) | ≈1e4 | ≈4e3 |
| 16: evals to reach fwd KL < 1e-6 | ≈250 | ≈100 | ≈400 | never (final 0.15) | not reliably (final 4e-3) | never (final 0.48) |

These results match the paper's trends:
- BaM converges to machine precision orders of magnitude faster than the gradient-based methods (ADVI, Score and Fisher, all with grid-searched ADAM learning rates).
- A larger batch makes BaM converge faster in gradient evaluations.
- GSM is competitive but slower than BaM with the larger batch.
- The Score method is the most erratic of the gradient-based methods.

D=64 and D=256 were not completed in the time available.

## Sec 5.1 — sinh-arcsinh targets (Fig 5.2 / E.4), D=10, 5 seeds
`figures/sinharcsinh_fkl.png`, `figures/sinharcsinh_rkl.png`. Only s=0.2 (10⁴ evaluations) and s=1.8 (5·10³ evaluations) finished, both with τ=1.

- **s=0.2, τ=1** (final forward KL / reverse KL):
  - BaM-5: 0.50 / 0.37
  - BaM-10: 0.52 / 0.36
  - GSM: 0.40 / 0.48
  - ADVI: 0.42 / 0.37
  - Score: 1.37 / 0.67
  - Fisher: 1.57 / 0.73

  BaM reaches its plateau in far fewer gradient evaluations than ADVI. Final reverse KL is similar for BaM and
  ADVI, and Score and Fisher are worse. This matches the paper.
- **s=1.8, τ=1** (5·10³ evaluations):
  - Forward KL is large for every method (BaM about 2·10³, ADVI 1.6·10³, GSM 1.2·10²). This is a hard, highly skewed target.
  - Reverse KL: BaM ≈ 9, ADVI ≈ 10, Fisher ≈ 11, Score ≈ 19.
  - GSM's reverse KL **diverges** (about 10¹²). The paper reports the same failure of GSM for highly skewed targets.
  - The paper also reports that BaM converges to a higher forward KL than the alternatives at large skew. We see the same thing relative to GSM.

## Sec 5.2 — posteriordb (Fig 5.3 / E.6): 5 seeds, 10⁵ gradient evaluations
`figures/posteriordb_rel_mean.png`, `figures/posteriordb_rel_sd.png`. Final relative mean error / relative SD error, as the mean over seeds:

| model | BaM-8 | BaM-32 | GSM-8 | GSM-32 | ADVI-8 | ADVI-32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| arK (nearly Gaussian) | 2.7 / 0.53 | **0.028 / 0.028** | 0.13 / 0.03 | 0.12 / 0.02 | 0.22 / 0.13 | 0.48 / 0.16 |
| gp_pois_regr | 36 / 1.6 | **0.35** / 1.19 | 0.57 / 0.87 | 0.53 / 0.87 | 14.7 / 8.2 | 13.5 / 12.8 |
| eight-schools centered | 0.33 / 1.09 | **0.32** / 1.07 | 0.38 / 0.77 | 0.40 / 0.75 | 0.55 / 0.80 | 0.53 / 0.79 |

Most of the paper's trends reproduce:
- BaM with B=32 reaches the lowest relative mean error on all three models.
  - On arK and the GP model, it converges in about 10³ evaluations, while ADVI needs more than 10⁴ evaluations or does not converge at all.
- BaM benefits strongly from the larger batch. GSM and ADVI do not.
- GSM oscillates or plateaus at a slightly higher error.
- On the hierarchical model, BaM learns the mean well but converges to a **larger relative SD error** than GSM and ADVI. The paper notes exactly this in Appendix E.5.

Where we deviate:
- BaM-8 with the decaying schedule λ_t = BD/(t+1) is slow on arK and the GP model and had not converged within
  10⁵ evaluations. On the GP model, one or more seeds did not converge, and the shaded band in the figure is wide.
- In the paper, BaM-8 is also the slowest BaM curve, but it reaches a low error by about 4·10⁵ evaluations.

## Sec 5.3 — VAE / CIFAR-10
Not run. The code is in `exp_vae.py` but it was not executed, so there are no results.
